replies.text:
The phrase "the Egyptian dialect of the Arabic language" is too long a phrase, so most Westerners simply say "Egyptian Arabic" or "Moroccan Arabic" or whatever. Naturally, you understood me, as everybody does. So I'll continue with the Western convention: It's concise and easy to understand.

You brought up a good point: Because Modern Standard Arabic has a more consistent grammar, it's better suited for deducing grammar, as per my experiment. However, I like the sound of Egyptian Arabic, and the sound of the language (or dialect) is one of my motivations for putting in the time to study it. But whatever I end up studying when the time comes, I will probably only dabble in it. My main focus is on East Asian languages because I live on the US West Coast, and they (especially Japanese) require a lot of my time! So it will be just an experiment, not a serious study of the language. As such, whether I study MSA or a dialect, I will probably only do so for a few months.

Thank you for your advice and encouragement, Amira. You reminded me of a good reason to choose MSA. However, I already bought the Glossika course for Egyptian Arabic. If I choose MSA, I'll have to select a different source for example sentences or I'll have to pay $30 per month for a Glossika subscription, as Glossika has switched to a subscription service. Thanks again for your advice.

replies.author: @andymounthood
replies.text:
Hi, everyone. Thanks for all of your input. I had only read the first few comments before today. I had no idea people were still replying to me! (Note: If anyone replies after this, I might not see it.)

Remember that I'm not learning Arabic in order to use it, but only for an experiment in figuring out the grammar by studying sentences via the Glossika course. I could have chosen any language available via Glossika: Swahili, Hungarian, etc. I want to choose a language which is unlike any I've ever studied, so I thought Arabic would make a good choice. The experiment will only last a few weeks, so I don't expect to learn much. And it doesn't matter whether I understand anyone or whether anyone understands me. I'll probably forget everything afterwards anyway.

OK, here's my update: Currently, Glossika only has courses for MSA and Egyptian Arabic. Amira A and Ramez Mahmoud gave good reasons for choosing MSA. Amira said that MSA has consistent grammar rules, but Egyptian doesn't. Ramez says that the Egyptian dialect includes "some English and ancient Egyptian language words." They convinced me to use MSA for my experiment.

Then I went to the Glossika website (which is free to try and then costs $30 per month) and studied the first 5 MSA sentences. But I ran into two problems: (1.) I selected the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) for the written form because I can't read the Arabic script--but the written words were longer than the audio ones! I didn't have this problem with other languages I've studied via Glossika. (2.) The speaker is female. I've heard that Arabic is spoken differently by men than by women. I sent Glossika a DM on Twitter asking them about the first problem, but haven't gotten a reply yet after 10 days. So MSA is not available. I have to choose Egyptian Arabic. But that's OK. I like the sound of the Egyptian dialect.

I had previously bought the Glossika Egyptian Arabic course (the old version, which consists of PDF and MP3 files). I tried it out and it didn't have either of the problems of the MSA course: The IPA text seems to match the audio exactly and the speaker is male. Thank you all for your good advice, but I have no choice now: I'll have to run my experiment with the Egyptian dialect.

Now I just have to learn the 5 sounds in Egyptian arabic which don't exist in English, and then I'll start my experiment.

شجن  
سجن 
How many letters in this word ? only 3 letters 
ش  ج  ن  in the first word
and 
س ج ن 
in the second word

an other example

it could be a a name or verb with the same forming letters 
Sajana سجن 
sijin  سجن 
note that word did changed as formation but the meaning has changed 
the first became a verb ( imprisoned in past tense ) and the second became  a name (  jail or prison)

and the pronunciation is the important part in this language , if  there is a little changing in accent , it will leads a little change in meaning .

good work, but few small notes just for sake of clarity:
1- it's true you don't need a verb to be to express your self in Arabic, but this doesn't reduce the hardness as for equivalent information will be embedded in the word to follow using the root system
2- speaking of the root system what you mentioned above is primarily a suffix and prefix examples a system that is common in many languages where you can still recognize the root word in the middle, while in Semitic systems the root word may undergo a dramatic change where letters are shuffled  and reordered within the template of the word making it hard to recognize the patterns for non native 

keep up the good work

Think of it through this example, a Brit says queue, but if he says this in America, he won't be understood (mostly). Hence, he has to know the word line to replace queue in his native dialect. This is the case in the Arabian world though differences are sharper and bigger.

comments.text: When you're coming from an Indo-European language, the grammar of Semitic languages such as Arabic is far from easy. I'm exposed on a daily basis to Maltese, another Semitic language (although with a lot of influence of Sicilian, Italian and English), and I've found it nigh impossible to wrap my head around. Yes, I know that "KTB" has to do with writing: "ktieb" is the word for book, and "kotba" the word for books. (The word for office is "uffiċċju", in which you can see the Italian/Sicilian influence.) But the seemingly random way that vowels define the actual meaning of the word is completely alien to someone used to an Indo-European grammar.

comments.text:
People, Arabic originally has nothing to do with Islam, Proto Arabic started to exist sometime between 5000 BCE and 2500 BCE or maybe much earlier. 
Many ancient varieties where written in Musannad alphabet which was common in Yemen (past) and now in Ethiopia and Jibouti, and later on, around 200-300 CE arabic adopted the Nabatean alphabet from Syriac alphabet.
Classical Arabic which is also included in quran was actually the dialect of Quraish tribe and has actually many syriac elements.
I believe that Arabic was born in southern Syria, or in the desert region between Babel (Iraq) and Southern Syria.
Vowels in Arabic are very simple, they are either long (written) or short (unwritten, but instead words are vowelized with symbols, Harakat).
Arabic poetry is so fascinating and difficult as well.
Grammar is something really difficult but very similar to other semitic langs. like Hebrew, Aramaic and Phoenician.
Until now, in many levantine countries like Syria, Lebanon and Jordan we use many many words and expressions from the past ancient languages, like Aramaic, phoenician and Syriac, and I was really surprised to known that many spoken and vulgar words in our contemporary syrian accent were actually formal in Aramaic and Syriac.

Well, about articles... No, there are no articles, but there are different endings for adjectives used somewhat similar to "a" and "the". For example, a comparison of English, Latvian and Russian:
a red apple - sarkans ābols - красное яблоко
the red apple - sarkanais ābols - красное яблоко
So, you see, it changes in Latvian, but there is absolutely no difference in Russian, so I really have troubles to explain to Russians how this should be applied, that one thing mean something in general, while the other means one particular thing, or I just say it's like English articles "a" and "the"... if that helps.  XD

comments.text:
One of the best reasons to learn Latvian is that it has some of the most beautiful songs in the world.  Their choral literature, in particular, is fantastic.  They host a Song and Dance Festival in Riga every five years, culminating in a grand concert with 12,000, or more, singers on stage.  They bring together the best singers, instrumentalists, conductors and choral compostions to create a spectacle of surpassing beauty and emotional power.  Check out the entire 2013 Song Concert at:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7IFFEO4UD4o&t=8s 
There are many highlights, but don't miss "Gaismas Pils" (The Castle of Light) by Jazeps Vitols, found at: 5: 41: 35.  This is probably the most moving of all the numbers, and one that has special meaning to the Latvian people.  The song relates the legend of a Castle of Light that sank into an ancient lake and would only arise from the depths when Latvians were once again masters of their own land.  For a people under the domination of the Evil Empire for 50 years, and that became free again in 1991, this has special meaning, and it is reflected in their singing.  
It is also the inspiration for and the name of the National Library of Latvia in Riga--how appropriate as the name of a library--a Castle of Light.

comments.author: @Philoglossos
comments.text:
All modern languages are equally old, because they all derive from earlier forms of the same language. Latvian is the second most conservative living Indo European language (that is, compared to all other Indo European languages, it has changed the second least after Lithuanian over the past ~5,000 years). However, this doesn't make it "older". Think about it like this - if two twins are born and one looks more like its great grandmother than the other, that twin isn't "older", it's just happened to inherit more features of its ancestor.


As for Sanskrit - no, Latvian and Lithuanian do not derive from Sanskrit. Latvian and Lithuanian are Baltic languages, derived ultimately from Proto Balto-Slavic which itself is derived from Proto Indo European. Sanskrit is an Indo-Iranian language, being the mother of most north Indian languages. Sanskrit is like an old aunt all other Indo European languages, not a parent. That said, because of some shared sound shifts and their highly conservative nature, many Latvian and Lithuanian words look very similar to their equivalent in Sanskrit. For example, all three languages changed original Indo European /o/ into /a/, so the word for a female sheep "*H₂ówis" becomes "áviḥ" in Sanskrit, "avis" in Lithuanian and "avs" in Latvian. Compare Latin "ovis" and English "ewe". Another shared sound shift is that palatal ḱ becomes ś~š~s, so PIE "*ḱwṓ" (dog) becomes "śvā́" in Sanskrit and "šuo" in Lithuanian. Compare English "hound" and Latin "canis".

comments.text:
There's no reason to learn Latvian. Even in Latvia they don't speak it. I'm Italian, and the first time in Riga I was afraid to speak Russian; when I moved there, I went at McDonald's, and, while I was thinking about my life, I heard clearly the waiters calling the orders: двадцать! Двадцать один! Пожалуйста! 

Everywhere I've been able to use my Russian.  As a linguistic, I really enjoyed learning Latvian: as you say, it retains many particularities of ancient languages, and some words are similar even to ancient Greek (for example one could guess immediately what does "melns" mean). But my teachers, who were Latvians, were not able to speak fluently Latvian, so I've been able to learn just the written language. In big cities like Riga or Daugavpils you can live and work knowing only Russian, as I did (of course I had to know immediately words like piens, olas,  maize, iela, veikals, lidosta...). I'm so sorry about it, once you learn Latvian, you can only love it. 
You're speaking the language of lido, of ancient rituals, of magic, immediately you turn back in medieval ages when you say a word in Latvian. I miss your country so much 😢💖🇱🇻 even the red of the flag is something wonderful, I miss even the snow in May!

I want to be able to read labels enough to cook without poisoning myself via allergies, and I recently started contracting for a Chinese company. That kicked me into bothering to add it to my study, at least to pick up some basics, and…I'm remembering it more easily and faster than I do Russian. Doesn't seem any harder than Greek, on that front.

I found one app (Pandarow) that includes a record-and-evaluate for pronunciation checks, which is a bit finicky about recording me but seems to do a decent job. I'm also using the Memrise English-to-Mandarin course. Both methods have their strengths and weaknesses. I ideally want the flash card method with everything Memrise does plus the audio with the characters (it often shows just pinyin, with the audio only being when it quizzes you on pinyin), so I'm still looking into options. One eventual goal is getting through HSK 1 & 2 on Clozemaster.

Familiarity with the Russian alphabet sure helps with the pinyin, though, and familiarity with Greek alphabet helped with the Russian. I think it's interesting, how details you know about one language can help with another, even if you don't know much.

comments.text:
I love your videos a lot and have been enjoying watching them for a while. However, there is something mentioned in this video which is not 100% accurate. The followings are my perspective as a linguist of East Asian languages.
The Chinese writing system is "morphosyllabic", which is close to what you described as "semanto phonetic". In Chinese, each character indicates an independent meaning, and in most of the situations, they function as morphemes. Meanwhile, each Chinese character is an individual syllable.
Why the seemingly non-phonetic Chinese writing system provides clues about sound is because over 90% of the characters are COMPOUNDS, which means they both have a semantic radical “部首” and a phonetic element “声旁”. The pictograms, logograms, and ideograms mentioned in the video only account for a very small proportion (less than 10%) of the writing system. A lot of pictograms, logograms, and ideograms don't indicate sounds. It is better to add semantic-phonetic COMPOUNDS to your description of the writing system because they are "mainstream".
Like your channel, looking forward to watching new videos!
